initial_requirements: Tarrant County needs an integrated justice capability to improve the administration of indigent defense services and information sharing across the criminal justice community. slots.key: Exception cases such as incomplete requests or conflicts
slots.value: Paused, rerouted, or escalated when anything breaks the normal flow, including missing information, a conflict, an attorney not meeting the qualification for that court or case type, workload limits being reached, or a special case needing supervisory review. If a county or justice-community source is unavailable or returns incomplete data, the appointment should not fail silently: staff should see a clear message that the data is unavailable or partial, and the request should either be held for follow-up or allowed to proceed only if policy says the missing piece is not essential. If the original attorney is formally withdrawing, there is a conflict, or the case circumstances have materially changed, the old appointment should be closed out first and a new one created. When the missing information is critical, staff should be blocked from completing the appointment and it should be held and escalated right away; when it is helpful but not essential, they should be allowed to continue with a visible warning and a note that the data was incomplete. The workflow should make it very clear what happened and what still needs to be resolved, and it should preserve the partial work so staff can finish it later without starting over. The key rule is whether the missing or uncertain information could change the legal correctness of the appointment: if it could affect the defendant’s rights, the appointed attorney’s authority, or compliance with court policy, staff must stop and escalate before changing anything; if it is noncritical and the appointment can still be completed accurately enough under policy, staff may proceed with the best available information and flag it for review.

slots.value: Staff can process the appointment themselves when they have the defendant’s identifying information, the case number or court information, the charge or case type, and enough data to match the request to the correct appointment pool. slots.key: Review routing and handoff workflow
slots.value: Reviews should route to the right staff or justice partner based on what is missing or needs clarification, rather than sitting in a queue, and the request should be sent back or forwarded to the appropriate place for correction or approval. Most often, the process starts when a defendant is identified as needing counsel in a criminal case, usually through the court process or after an intake or custody event. The request may be initiated by court staff, and in some situations jail staff or another justice partner may provide the information that causes the request to be created. The person or office that identified the missing information should be able to send it back with a reason, and the request should stay open until the needed items are provided or the case is formally closed out. If it can’t be completed right away, it should move into a pending or held state with a clear explanation of what’s blocking it and who is responsible for the next action. Alerts or reminders should be used so it doesn’t sit there unnoticed.

slots.key: Day-to-day maintenance ownership and issue resolution
slots.value: Day-to-day ownership should sit with the county, probably through the Office of Attorney Appointments or whichever IT support group they designate, because they’re the ones running the process every day. The vendor should handle defects, configuration support, and upgrades for anything inside the solution itself, while justice-community partners would mainly own corrections to the data or services they provide. Ownership shifts only when the issue sits outside the county’s control, such as a partner system outage, a data feed problem, or when a vendor fix is needed versus a business process fix. For anything in the gray area, the county should coordinate the handoff so staff always know who is responsible and nothing gets dropped. If a source is down or returns incomplete data during appointment processing, staff should see a clear message that the data is unavailable or partial, the request should be held for follow-up or allowed to proceed only if policy says the missing piece is not essential, the system should keep a record of what was attempted and what came back so staff can retry later without redoing the whole request, and critical-source failures should trigger escalation or an alert to the county support team right away. Staff should handle routine corrections, missing case details, simple routing mistakes, and normal appointment updates if they have the information and authority to do it. Anything involving a system outage, integration failure, data mismatch they can’t verify, or an issue owned by another agency should go to the vendor or the justice-community partner. If responsibility isn’t obvious, the handoff should go to the party that controls the source of truth for the data or process, with a clear escalation path and a notes trail explaining why it was routed there.

slots.key: Mandatory approval criteria before attorney assignment
slots.value: Before approval, staff need enough verified information to confirm the defendant identity, the correct case, the court making the request, and that the person appears eligible for appointed counsel. The request must also be complete enough for staff to assign an attorney without guessing about the charge, location, or special handling notes. Staff should also check for attorney conflicts or assignment restrictions, whether the case requires a special appointment process because of the charge, court, or custody situation, and now also the attorney pool's qualifications, language ability, and any special court assignment requirements. At a minimum, the intake must include the defendant’s identity, the case or cause number, the court, the charge or case type, custody status, contact or location information, and whatever indigency or appointment details the court requires. New staff should also be trained to identify incomplete or emergency requests, verify eligibility and conflicts, and use a clear checklist to decide when they can process routine requests independently versus when they need a supervisor. The job aid should also spell out the basic decision boundaries first: what counts as a complete request, what fields are mandatory for each request type, and which attorney pools or rotations can be used for that case. The request should stay on the standard path when it is complete, the case type is clear, the defendant and court details match, and the next attorney in rotation is eligible and available. Timely, fair, and consistent processing is a baseline expectation for the workflow. Staff should be able to process it themselves when they have the defendant’s identifying information, the case number or court information, the charge or case type, and enough data to match the request to the correct appointment pool. Staff need to confirm the request is complete enough to identify the person, the case, and the type of appointment needed, and then check for any obvious conflicts or restrictions. slots.key: Attorney assignment rotation and workload balancing rules
slots.value: Attorney assignment is usually driven by the court and case type, starting with the next attorney in the approved rotation or pool for that court and case type, as long as they are eligible and available. If an attorney has a conflict, is not qualified, or has too high a workload, staff should skip that attorney and move to the next eligible one rather than forcing the assignment. The job aid should also make clear that an attorney who is unavailable or over workload limits is a stop condition for normal processing. The next attorney in rotation must be eligible and available for the request to stay on the standard path. Staff must also confirm that the next attorney in the rotation is eligible for that court and case type, not conflicted, and not blocked by workload or other assignment limits.

topics.topic_content: Protection of sensitive justice and personal information

slots.key: Access control rules for case, defendant, and appointment data
slots.value: Only users with a specific case- or appointment-related need should access the data, and queries should be tied to a specific case or appointment need rather than broad searching. The default should be minimal access. If the source contains sealed, juvenile, or otherwise restricted information, that content should be blocked from coming through or limited to users with proper authority and a documented reason to view it, with tighter controls and approvals only when the law or court rules require it. Tighter limits should also apply for sealed matters, juvenile cases, and any stage where the user does not need the data to complete the appointment; some roles should only see a subset of information, and some queries may need to be blocked entirely if they exceed role authorization. Sensitive items should be restricted based on role, case type, and any legal or court-imposed confidentiality rules, and the system should expose only the minimum necessary information when a request is reviewed or routed.

slots.key: Acceptance conditions for successful appointment processing and notifications
slots.value: Acceptance conditions include confirming that the request is complete enough to identify the person, the case, and the type of appointment needed, and then checking for any obvious conflicts or restrictions. If the case details are clear and the appointment authority is straightforward, it can be assigned right away. If something is missing, inconsistent, or the matter belongs to a different court, office, or appointment path, it should be routed or held until the missing information is resolved. Sealed, juvenile, or other special-restriction issues trigger extra review before anyone moves forward. If the appointed attorney needs to be changed later because of a conflict, withdrawal, reassignment, or another case change, staff should be able to replace the attorney without losing the original appointment history, capture the reason for the change, update the current active appointment, notify affected parties, and close out the old appointment cleanly before the new one becomes active when applicable. When replacing an appointed attorney, an in-place amendment is appropriate only for a correction or straightforward substitution with no break in representation, when the case, court, and assignment basis stay the same and the system preserves original history while updating the active attorney. If the original attorney is formally withdrawing, there is a conflict, or the case circumstances have materially changed, the old appointment should be closed out first and a new one created. Approval rules should follow the applicable court or county policy for that appointment type, especially when judge or supervisor sign-off is required before the change becomes effective. When a replacement attorney change needs approval, it should depend on the type of case, the stage of the case, and the reason for the replacement. If the change affects a court-appointed assignment, involves withdrawal for cause, or there is any policy requirement tied to a specific court or judge, judicial approval would likely be needed before it takes effect. For more routine administrative substitutions, a supervisor or appointments staff approval may be enough if county policy allows it. The rule for proceeding versus escalating should be explicit: if missing or uncertain information could change the legal correctness of the appointment, affect the defendant’s rights, the appointed attorney’s authority, or compliance with court policy, staff should stop and escalate before changing anything. If it is a noncritical detail and the appointment can still be completed accurately enough under policy, staff may proceed with the best available information and flag it for review.

slots.key: Access control and transfer restrictions for sensitive case information
slots.value: Access should be restricted based on role, case type, and any legal or court-imposed confidentiality rules. Sealed information, juvenile matters, protected witness information, and other details the court says should only be seen by specific people must not be broadly visible or included in general notifications. When a request is reviewed or routed, the system should expose only the minimum necessary information to each person involved, and if a sensitive item must be flagged for action it should be masked or summarized so the workflow can continue without disclosing the underlying detail to users who do not have clearance.

Masking is appropriate when users only need to confirm identity or case linkage, not full details. Transfers outside the normal approved workflow or involving a non-county party should be explicitly reviewed and authorized first.
